time.title: The first Sanborn map
time.note: The earliest fire-insurance map of the city. Its buildings now gone are traced here in the map's own colors.

curated.name: What was left of the Great Basin in 1886, between 9th and 10th Streets
curated.note: The water marked "Basin" in the block between 9th and 10th Streets, Byrd and Canal, on the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 11), its outline read from the sheet and placed by the corners of 10th and Byrd, 11th and Byrd and 11th and Canal, as the sheet's traced buildings are. By then rail yards and warehouses covered the rest of the basin. Drawn 1880 to 1895: the start is the marker's "1880s", the end the next map's year, both approximate. Still water at its own level, with a smooth bank, on today's ground.

curated.name: Basin between 11th and 12th Streets, 1886
curated.note: The narrow water marked "Basin" beside the track and trestle on the east side of Byrd Street between 11th and 12th, on the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 11), placed as the entry above. Years approximate, as above.

curated.name: James River and Kanawha Canal, from Tredegar to the Great Basin
curated.note: The canal's last mile into the Great Basin. Its middle stretch, between 6th and 7th Streets, is read from the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 10, "Old James River & Kanawha Canal (Mill Canal)"), placed by the corners of 6th and Byrd, 7th and Byrd and 7th and Canal. West of it the line runs straight to the east end of the canal's dry bed by Tredegar mapped in OpenStreetMap (w307593380), and east of it straight to the basin's west corner, as the 1886 key map shows it: those two runs are approximate. Drawn about 10 m wide (sheet 10 draws it about 8 m) from 1800, the basin's year, to 1895, the end of the basin entries; the railroad laid on its towpath from 1880 is not drawn.

curated.name: The canal's last stretch into what was left of the basin, 1886
curated.note: From the basin's old west corner to the water left between 9th and 10th Streets, as the 1886 Sanborn key map shows the canal running into it: a straight line, approximate.

curated.name: Free Bridge (the Ninth Street Bridge)
curated.note: The free road bridge from the foot of 9th Street to Manchester, opened in June 1873 (RVA Mag; Dogtown Dish dates the span it describes to 1878, after the flood of 1877) and closed after the floods of 1969 and 1972, when the Manchester Bridge replaced it. Built "rather low over the river": its deck is drawn 8 m over the water, an assumption. Its line is today's Manchester Bridge's, which the USGS 1:24,000 Richmond quadrangle of 1934 shows it on ("9th St Bridge", just downstream of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge), from the corner of 9th Street to the foot of Commerce Road in Manchester: approximate. Drawn only in builds made with --with next: the 1925 and 1950 prints (version 4) were drawn before it.

curated.name: Libby Prison (warehouses, 1845–52; prison 1862–65)
curated.note: Three brick warehouses, each 110 × 44 ft and four stories, on the east side of 20th Street between Cary and Dock. Used as a Confederate prison 1862–65; dismantled in 1889 and re-erected in Chicago. Footprint from the published dimensions, placed at the corner; not surveyed.

curated.name: Shockoe Creek (open stream)
curated.note: The creek ran open between present-day 15th and 16th Streets, dividing the town. A culvert begun in 1877 enclosed part of it, but the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, key map and sheets 18 and 19) still draws it open from Broad Street to the Dock, so it is drawn to 1890 (the end approximate). Course approximated as midway between the two streets.

curated.name: Richmond and Petersburg (Atlantic Coast Line) approach to Byrd Street Station
curated.note: The track from the north end of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge (OSM w710689016) across the Haxall Canal into Byrd Street Station at Seventh and Byrd Streets, the R&P's original Richmond station and later the Atlantic Coast Line's headquarters, closed in 1958. Today nothing of it is mapped north of the bridge. Approximate: one track along the middle of the station's throat, read by eye from the USGS 1:24,000 Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 (which show the line crossing the canal and fanning into the station yard between Seventh and Eighth Streets south of Byrd) and joined to the bridge's mapped end, about 20 m east of where the maps put it. Drawn with the bridge, from 1838 to 1970 (the R&P's depot stood at 8th and Byrd before Byrd Street Station, and the 1886 Sanborn map, volume 1, sheet 10, shows its tracks fanning in between 7th and 9th south of Canal); the years are the bridge's, not the track's.

curated.name: Chesapeake and Ohio approach to the Church Hill Tunnel
curated.note: The C&O's line to the Church Hill Tunnel's west portal, by 18th Street just north of Marshall: it left the old Virginia Central line west of 17th Street and curved southeast. The tunnel opened in 1873, collapsed on October 2, 1925, and its western end was sealed the following spring, so it is drawn through 1925 and not after. Its course: OSM's abandoned branch (w169784705) from the junction with today's Peninsula Subdivision south to 17th Street; then the C&O spur shown on the 1924–25 Sanborn map, volume 1, sheet 24, crossing the block between 17th and 18th Streets, Marshall and Clay, between the Richmond Cold Storage and International Harvester warehouses (the sheet fitted to the four corners of the block, to about a meter, and the line set midway between the warehouses standing today); then straight across 18th Street to the portal mapped in OSM (the tunnel, w6036486). Approximate.
